Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: ok hey everyone thanks for joining, uh welcome to this week's poc caching sync for NovaHealth. we're gonna review the numbers Ethan pulled and then talk next steps.
[00:14] Carlos: yeah thanks, appreciate it. just quick note, we had a big spike monday so some numbers might look a bit off but overall happy to dig in.
[00:24] Ethan: cool, i'll share screen, give me one sec — all right pulling up the latest dashboard. so on the last run we saw prefix cache hit at 72 percent, kv cache at 48 percent, average token latency dropped roughly 12 percent when the cache hit, and cost per 1k tokens decreased accordingly.
[00:42] Priya: 72% sounds pretty good, is that for full prompts or prefix only? i thought we were tracking template matches.
[00:52] Ethan: good question. that's prefix matches — so the runtime matched the leading token sequences we've been storing. template matches (after canonicalization) are only about 37 percent right now, that explains the kv delta.
[01:10] Liam: when you say kv cache can you remind me how Redwood's kv is scoped? is it per model, per route, per customer?
[01:19] Maya: yeah so quick refresher — the cache has two layers in our setup: prefix cache for identical leading tokens, and kv cache for reused key-value states across sequences. in your POC we scoped KV to the route+model pair and a 24 hour TTL by default, but that was tuned to a small window to avoid stale context.
[01:39] Carlos: got it, and eviction policy? LRU?
[01:42] Ethan: yep LRU with weighted size-based eviction. we also have optional pinning for high-value keys if you want to reserve slots for warm prefixes.
[01:52] Priya: could you run through a few examples where prefix hit fails — is it just punctuation/case mismatches?
[01:58] Ethan: mostly — whitespace, punctuation, minor param shuffles. also we saw a lot of small personalization tokens at the front of prompts (e.g., user name or session id) which breaks prefix matching. that's why canonicalization is important.
[02:15] Carlos: yeah we saw that — our product team tends to prepend user id or locale which is low value; we can probably move it into metadata instead.
[02:23] Maya: perfect, that's exactly the kind of change that'll push template match rates up.
[02:28] Ethan: on the KV side, hits are lower because a lot of requests diverge mid-stream even if prefix matches. two approaches: increase kv cache TTL and size to keep more KVs, or improve prompt normalization so more requests produce identical cache keys. both have cost/latency tradeoffs.
[02:45] Priya: what's the rough cost impact if we bump KV retention?
[02:49] Ethan: ballpark: doubling TTL and doubling memory allocation would increase infra spend in that layer about 15 to 25 percent depending on utilization, but you'd see token-level cost drop because fewer model steps are recomputed.
[03:02] Liam: can you quantify how much latency gains we get?
[03:06] Ethan: on hits we saw P50 drop from ~120ms to ~85ms, P95 improved from ~620ms to ~410ms in the cached scenario on our recent runs. so it's meaningful for tail latency.
[03:19] Carlos: those P95s are close to our target but we'd like under 400ms. any ideas?
[03:24] Ethan: a few: 1) improve canonicalization so more requests hit prefix/kv, 2) route reads to a smaller model variant for warm-cache responses, 3) increase batch sizes on the backend a bit if latency SLO permits.
[03:38] Maya: to add, Redwood Dedicated can be used for predictable throughput if you find hosted bursts cause misses; but i know NovaHealth is sensitive about data residency so we can also do private deployment.
[03:49] Priya: yeah we want to avoid private if possible but may go Dedicated. need to review compliance docs first.
[03:55] Maya: i'll send the SOC2 and network diagram after this call.
[03:59] Carlos: awesome.
[04:02] Ethan: back to the prompt work — we recommended a canonicalization pipeline we sketched last week: strip low-value prefixes (ids, timestamps), normalize whitespace/punctuation, replace variable tokens with placeholders, and then hash the canonicalized prompt to generate cache keys.
[04:19] Priya: that hashing step — is that deterministic across models? we have multi-model routing.
[04:24] Ethan: yes we include model id and route in the cache key so it's unique. the hash is stable as long as the canonicalization rules are stable. be mindful when you change templates.
[04:34] Carlos: our concern is losing precision — if we canonicalize too aggressively we might change the user's response. is there a risk?
[04:41] Ethan: we're only canonicalizing input tokens that are not semantically relevant — ids, system timestamps, known tracking tokens. anything you mark as required will be left intact. canonicalization is configurable per route.
[04:55] Priya: okay that helps. what about prompt reuse strategy — are we encouraging more templated prompts from our product side?
[04:59] Maya: yes, templating + placeholder substitution is the best path for cache friendliness. if you can produce consistent prompt skeletons, hit rates go way up.
[05:08] Liam: operationally, how will we monitor regressions? any alerts?
[05:12] Ethan: we can add an alert on sudden drop in prefix hit-rate or a spike in model tokens per minute. we also track per-route P95 latency and will create a dashboard card for 15-min rolling hit rate.
[05:25] Priya: perfect.
[05:27] Maya: quick question — last run included anonymized sample traces in the dashboard, can you confirm we don't store PII in cache keys?
[05:35] Ethan: yep keys are hashed and we strip user-identifying fields by default; still, we recommend you avoid embedding raw PII in the prompt start.
[05:44] Carlos: will share the sample dataset but we'll scrub identifiers first.
[05:48] Priya: timeline — is two weeks enough to see improvement after canonicalization?
[05:53] Ethan: typically yes — you'll see a lift in prefix hit within a few days once canonicalization is applied; KV will lag as it needs repeated identical sequences. we recommended a 2-4 week observation window.
[06:06] Maya: for the benchmark run, Ethan will run the 20k query synthetic that mixes your traffic distribution and report delta in hit rate, cost, and latency.
[06:16] Carlos: and if we want to push latency under 400ms p95 what's the recommended change set?
[06:20] Ethan: start with canonicalization and template enforcement, then increase KV retention + pinning for highest value keys, then if needed move to Dedicated capacity or a warm model routing for tail-critical routes.
[06:33] Priya: are there any quick wins we can implement on our side this week?
[06:37] Carlos: we can remove user id from prompt prefix and move it to metadata — i'll try to have that rolled by end of week.
[06:44] Priya: i'll confirm the success metric and share with Maya.
[06:47] Maya: great.
[06:49] Ethan: a small note on metrics — 'hit' classification in the dashboard is inferred from token-level overlap heuristics and occasionally flags false-negatives; we'll add a 'confidence' column in the CSV we share.
[07:03] Carlos: excellent.
[07:05] Maya: ok let's talk about edge cases — multi-turn conversations where the prefix changes because of assistant follow-ups. any tips?
[07:12] Ethan: we use session-scoped KV caching for multi-turn. if the assistant emits a deterministic system sentence, that can be cached as well. canonicalization helps but sometimes you need to segment the conversation into smaller cacheable units.
[07:28] Priya: hmm segmentation might be a product change; we should weigh that.
[07:32] Liam: can Redwood provide code snippets for the canonicalization lib?
[07:36] Maya: yes Ethan has a reference python lib and a node snippet. we'll drop links.
[07:40] Ethan: i'll put those in the follow-up email with an example that transforms your current prompt style.
[07:46] Priya: thanks.
[07:48] Carlos: any security or compliance blockers we should expect?
[07:52] Maya: nothing unusual — SOC2, encrypted-at-rest keys, KMS integration for Private/Dedicated. i'll include the network diagram and the shared responsibility doc.
[07:59] Priya: perfect.
[08:01] Ethan: one more perf note — we saw some regressions when the model switched to longer context windows; kernel selection introduced a bit more latency on that path. we can pin an optimized kernel for your common sequence length to avoid that.
[08:18] Carlos: good to know.
[08:21] Maya: ok wrapping up — recap next steps?
[08:25] Priya: confirm success metric (Priya)
[08:27] Carlos: export sample traffic and scrub PII (Carlos)
[08:29] Ethan: run benchmark and share results (Ethan)
